PASSO 1: O alemão marca a função no arti: STEP 1: German marks the role on the article — but only in the masculine. That's the whole trap: STEP 2: only the masculine changes. So just ask whether the word is a der word. If it isn't, nothing happens.
O português descobre quem é sujeito e qu: English works out who does what from word order: "the man sees the dog" and "the dog sees the man" are different because the order changes — "the" never changes. German keeps the order freer and marks the object on the article instead: «Den Hund sieht der Mann» still means "the man sees the dog". You already know the idea from English pronouns: he sees → sees him. German does the same with masculine articles: der → den.
O acusativo: o objeto direto muda só no: The accusative: the direct object changes only in the masculine
O alemão tem quatro casos. Por agora voc: German has four cases. For now you need two: the NOMINATIVE (who does the action) and the ACCUSATIVE (the direct object: what you eat, drink, buy or have). The only difference between them is in the MASCULINE singular: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same. Verbs that take the accusative: essen, trinken, kaufen, haben, nehmen, möchten, lesen, sehen.
o português não muda o artigo: «o queijo: English "the" never changes: "the cheese" is the same as subject or object. German changes only the masculine: «der Käse» (subject) × «den Käse» (object) — the same switch as he → him.

«Ich möchte» é «eu gostaria» ou «eu quer: «Ich möchte» is "I'd like" — more polite than «ich will», which is closer to "I want" (and never means "I will"!). The modal verb goes in 2nd position and the other verb goes to the END, in the infinitive: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken» — literally "I'd like a coffee drink". This is the sentence "bracket". If the meaning is clear, the second verb can be left out: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee.» To order: «Ich nehme …» (I'll have …), «Ich möchte …», «Die Rechnung, bitte» and «Zahlen, bitte» (the check, please).
em português «eu gostaria de beber um ca: English keeps the verbs together: "I'd like to drink a coffee". German splits them and sends the second verb to the end: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken». And there's no "to": just the infinitive.

Tisch é masculino e recebe a ação de kau: Tisch is masculine and receives the action of kaufen as a direct object in the accusative. The article changes from der to den: Ich kaufe den Tisch.
Tisch é o sujeito da oração. No nominati: Tisch is the subject of the sentence. In the masculine nominative singular, use der: Der Tisch ist neu.
Schlüssel é masculino e é objeto direto: Schlüssel is masculine and the direct object of suchen. Among the options, the accusative form is den: Ich suche den Schlüssel.
Auto é neutro e é objeto direto de brauc: Auto is neuter and the direct object of brauchen. The indefinite article in the neuter accusative singular is ein: Wir brauchen ein Auto.
Hund é masculino e é objeto direto de ha: Hund is masculine and the direct object of haben. In the masculine accusative singular, ein becomes einen: Er hat einen Hund.
Em Das ist ein Stuhl, o nome que identif: In Das ist ein Stuhl, the noun after sein describes the subject, so it stays in the nominative — just as English says "it is he", not "him", in formal style. Stuhl is masculine singular: ein.
Besuchen recebe objeto direto no acusati: Besuchen takes a direct object in the accusative. To ask about the person visited, use wen — the German "whom"; wer ("who") would ask about the subject.
Lieben takes a direct object in the accusative. Du becomes dich ("you" as object): Ich liebe dich.
Suchen takes a direct object in the accusative. Ich becomes mich ("me"): Tom sucht mich.

O pronome sie no plural mantém a forma s: Plural sie stays sie in the accusative ("they" → "them" is the same word in German). So: Wir besuchen sie.

Hören pede objeto direto no acusativo. O: Hören takes a direct object in the accusative. Wir becomes uns ("us"): Hörst du uns?
